summary: This program builds a list of farmers-market products and then uses three stream pipelines to answer questions about them: which vendors exist, what one vendor sells and for how much, and what those prices would be after a 10% discount.

lines.text: Collectors supplies the ready-made recipes, such as toSet() and toList(), that gather the results of a stream back into a collection.
The list is declared as List but created as an ArrayList, so the rest of the code depends only on the general list behaviour.
Several products share the vendor "Baker's Lane" so that the filtering pipelines later have more than one match to work with.
A Set is the right container for vendor names because it automatically drops the duplicates that come from vendors with several products.
Storing the vendor name in a variable means the same value drives both the menu and the discount pipeline, with no risk of a typo in one of them.
forEach walks the finished list and hands each string to println; the :: syntax is a method reference, a compact way of saying "call this method on each item."
The discount is passed in as a fraction rather than hard-coded, so the same method can apply any percentage off.
stream() turns the list into a flow of elements that the following operations can transform one step at a time, leaving the original list untouched.
map replaces each product in the stream with the result of calling getVendor on it, so a stream of products becomes a stream of vendor names.
This guard discards missing or empty vendor names before they reach the set, so bad data never shows up in the report.
collect ends the pipeline by pouring the surviving names into a Set, which keeps only one copy of each vendor.
filter keeps only the products whose vendor matches, and equalsIgnoreCase means differences in capitalisation do not cause a miss.
Each matching product is mapped to a display string, with %.2f forcing the price to show exactly two decimal places like real money.
Converting the discount into a multiplier once, before the stream starts, avoids repeating the same subtraction for every product.
The price is multiplied by the factor to apply the discount, and Math.max keeps the result from ever dipping below zero.
